title: Practice runs and evidence
target: Use repeated trials to prepare an evidence-based design explanation.
criteria: Measure the actual course distance and run times.
Calculate average speed and describe variation.
Choose a final change supported by repeated evidence.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A practice lane is measured as 3.6 m. A car takes 4.5 s from its start line to its finish line. What is average speed?
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A team times motion over 2.5 m but divides the full 5 m course by that time. What must be corrected?
options: Use the distance between the actual timing start and stop points.
Double the recorded time without evidence.
Keep 5 m because larger distances give better scores.
Replace measured time with the prediction.
cpa.guide: Distance and elapsed time must describe the same interval.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: Example times over the same 4.8 m path are 6.0, 6.4, and 5.6 s. What does the spread show?
options: Performance or measurement varies, so one run is not the whole picture.
The car’s speed is exactly identical in every run.
All three readings must be discarded.
The slowest run is automatically a mistake.
cpa.guide: Repeated results reveal variation. Diagnose it rather than selecting a convenient result.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A 4.2 m run takes 7.0 s. A second run on the same path takes 6.0 s. Which comparison is correct?
options: Average speed falls from 0.70 to 0.60 m/s.
Speed doubles because time falls by 1 s.
Both averages are 4.2 m/s.
Average speed rises from 0.60 to 0.70 m/s.
cpa.guide: 4.2/7 = 0.60 and 4.2/6 = 0.70; compare rates, not time differences alone.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: After removing a wheel rub, three example times improve from about 8 s to about 6 s over the same track. Which choice is supported?
options: Undo it because lower time means lower speed.
Declare a guaranteed win on every surface.
Keep the adjustment provisionally and confirm it with the same controlled test.
Credit a different change that was not made.
cpa.guide: Repeated faster times support the tested adjustment, within the tested conditions.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: A team changes the battery and wheel size together and gets one faster run. What can it conclude?
options: Wheel size alone caused the improvement.
The combined setup was faster in that run; it cannot isolate the wheel effect.
The battery had no effect.
One run proves all future results.
cpa.guide: Multiple simultaneous changes confound causal attribution. Isolate one factor and repeat.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
